Verify rewrite DATA ONLY. Do not write improved examples or solve the user's task.
Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

on tuesday, march 12, i visited maple basket at 41 larch avenue in riverbend to sit in on the morning handoff and follow part of one grocery route. i got there at 8:20, before the first van left. mara chen, who owns the shop, was at the packing counter with luis ortega, the dispatcher, and nia brooks, a driver. dev patel, the building superintendent, came down from the apartments next door a little later. the plan was to look at how an order moved from the store to a customer's door, not to review the whole delivery service. there were twelve orders on nia's route that were marked for delivery by 9:30, and several more waiting for another driver.

the shop is narrow in front but has a long packing area behind the counter. two wheeled racks were set beside the back door, one with green labels for produce and the other with orange labels for frozen bags. the labels had the route stop number and a short customer name, but not a full address. luis checked them against a paper route sheet, and nia checked the temperature tags while she loaded. she said she usually starts with the frozen bags because they are easier to keep together, though she sometimes changes the order if a customer has asked for a particular drop-off time. mara said the printer had been feeding two copies of some labels since monday. it had not happened on every order, so she was keeping the spare labels in a small envelope rather than throwing them away.

1. things we checked during the handoff
- whether the stop number on the bag matched the paper route sheet
- which bags needed to stay in the insulated carrier
- what the driver could see about the drop-off instructions

nia paused at order seven because the route sheet said “leave at side entrance,” while the bag label only showed apartment 5B. she asked, “do you know if that means the entrance by the laundry room?” luis said, “the note came through exactly that way, and i haven't got a second note.” dev had not heard which entrance the customer meant. nia put the order back on the rack for a minute while luis looked at the dispatch screen, then she placed it in the van's front cooler. nobody said which entrance would be used, and we moved on to the other bags. mara also pointed out that one produce bag had a sticker marked “keep upright,” because a jar of sauce was packed beside the greens. the sticker was intact, but the bag was leaning against a crate when i first saw it.

at 8:38, nia started the route. i rode with her for the first few stops, with permission from the shop, and luis stayed behind to handle calls. the paper sheet listed stops in a numbered sequence, but the dispatch screen showed a slightly different order for the two buildings on alder street. nia said the screen can shift a stop when the expected travel time changes, and she normally checks both versions before leaving. for this trip she followed the paper sequence, because it was already loaded into her route notes. the first delivery was a small order at a duplex on birch lane. she set the bags inside the covered porch after checking the note, “please use the left door; dog in yard.” the dog was not outside while we were there. she took a photo of the bags at the left door, and the app showed the delivery time as 8:46.

we reached the alder street apartments a few minutes later. the main entrance mat was wet, and nia asked me, “could we use the side entry if it is open?” i couldn't tell from outside whether it was open, and dev, who had met us there, said the side door sometimes latched behind people. while we waited, a notice on the elevator said it would be unavailable for inspection from 8:40 to 8:47. nia carried two bags up the stairs to the third floor. she kept the frozen order inside the insulated carrier and left the produce order beside the marked apartment door, as its note requested. the building was quiet, except for a cart rolling somewhere above us. dev held the stairwell door while she went back for the second bag.

the order for 5B was still in the van when we came downstairs. nia read the note again and said, “i can leave it by the side entrance if that's what they want, but i don't want to guess at the wrong door.” luis called her at 9:02 and said he was trying the customer number shown on the screen. i could hear only nia's side of the call; she said, “okay, i'll wait here a moment.” she did not take the bag out of the cooler during the call. after that, she checked the other stop on the block, which was for apartment 2A and had a clear instruction to leave the groceries with the concierge. the concierge was at the desk, and nia handed over two bags. she asked for the order name, and he checked it against a small tablet before taking them.

back at the shop, mara showed me the paper envelope for the duplicate labels and the route sheet with two handwritten marks beside the alder street stops. she said the marks were there because the order sequence on paper and on the screen did not match, not because either order had been changed. luis returned to the packing counter and answered a call about a missing bag of pears; i did not hear whether that call was connected to nia's route. before i left, nia was checking the cooler temperature display and writing the reading in the driver's log. the time beside her entry was 9:18, and the next line on the page was blank.", "output": "On Tuesday, March 12, I visited Maple Basket at 41 Larch Avenue in Riverbend to observe the morning handoff and follow part of a grocery route. Do not add a greeting, subject, signature, conclusion, or fact that the input did not supply.", "input": "i started keeping notes on the lunches at ridgeview middle school in september, mostly because my daughter mara kept coming home with a very specific account of what she had eaten and what she had traded away. after six weeks i went through the notes and wrote this review. i am not reviewing every meal the school serves, because i was only able to visit the cafeteria on tuesdays and thursdays, and some of the menus changed when deliveries were late. still, i saw enough to get a sense of the routine, and mara's stories filled in a few gaps.

the cafeteria is a wide, bright room with long windows along the east wall. students come in through two doors, collect a tray, and move past the hot-food counter before they reach the salad station and milk coolers. the line looks slow at first, but it moves fairly steadily once everyone knows which side to join. on the first day i visited, a sign telling students to take one fruit was partly hidden behind a stack of cups. a staff member moved it before the next lunch period. the tables were clean when i arrived, though the noise made it difficult to hear conversations from more than a few seats away.

the best meal i tried was a baked potato bar. the potatoes were hot and soft inside, and students could add shredded cheese, black beans, or a spoonful of broccoli. the toppings were in separate metal pans, which meant a student who disliked one item could leave it off without making a fuss. mara said, “the potato is better when you get cheese and beans together.” i agreed, although the cheese was cold enough that it did not melt much. there was also a small whole-grain roll. it was a little dry, but still useful for wiping up the beans at the end.

the tomato soup and grilled cheese day was less even. the sandwich had browned edges and a crisp bottom, but the middle was cool by the time i sat down. i could not tell whether that was because the sandwiches had been waiting or because i took too long getting a drink. the soup was warm, not hot, and tasted mostly of tomato and basil. two students at the next table said it was “fine, just not like home,” which struck me as a fair description. mara ate the soup but traded half her sandwich for apple slices. i do not know if the other student thought that was a good deal.

1. the small details that shape lunch

the salad station was a stronger feature than i expected. it usually had romaine, cucumber rounds, shredded carrots, and one additional item that changed from day to day, such as corn or chickpeas. the vegetables looked fresh on both visits when i used the station, and the tongs were easy for younger students to handle. dressing came in little sealed cups, with ranch and Italian available. there was no sign explaining whether students could take more than one cup. i watched one student ask, and the lunch aide said, “take what you’ll use.” that simple answer seemed to prevent an argument.

the fruit choices were less predictable. apples and bananas appeared on every day i visited, but on one tuesday the pears were bruised, and mara left hers untouched. another week there were orange wedges, which she liked, although they were still cold from storage. the milk cooler offered plain and chocolate milk. it was sometimes crowded, because it sits just past the point where students turn toward the tables. i saw a few students step back into the line to reach it. moving the cooler a little farther along might help, but i do not know whether the room has space for that.

the staff made a noticeable difference to the overall experience. one lunch aide greeted students by name and reminded them to grab a fork without making the reminder sound like a scolding. another staff member helped a student open a carton, then went back to wiping a table. during my second visit, a tray slipped near the entrance and a few grapes rolled under a bench. the staff member nearest the door brought a broom over quickly, while students waited for the walkway to be clear. Nobody seemed upset, and the line continued. The lunch period was short enough that small delays mattered, but the adults kept things moving without rushing students through their food.

there are limits to what i could judge from these visits. i did not see breakfast, and i was not there on days with pasta, tacos, or the chicken sandwich that mara mentions most often. i also do not know how much of each meal is prepared at school rather than delivered. the printed menu was helpful, but the descriptions did not always say what sides were included. on the soup day, for example, the menu listed “grilled cheese and tomato soup” without mentioning the apple slices. That is a small omission, but it made it harder for me to know what students would actually be offered.

overall, ridgeview's lunch has some good options and a few details that could work better. the potato bar and salad station gave students room to choose, while the cooler placement and uneven fruit quality stood out as practical problems. i would like to see the menu describe the sides more fully and the cold items checked before lunch begins. mara still has days when she comes home hungry, but she also talks about meals she enjoyed and things she wants to try again. from what i saw, the cafeteria is doing several things well, even if the experience is not equally good every day.", "output": "I started keeping notes on the lunches at Ridgeview Middle School in September, mostly because my daughter, Mara, kept coming home with a very specific account of what she had eaten and what she had traded away.
